interactions.summary: A student agrees with the prior answer, another student tries to explain the Jephthah paradox through free will as a preventive gift from God, and Jiang rejects that as insufficient before restating the paradox and asking whether Dante is taking a jab at the Church.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Students testing the paradox with Jiang pressure

interactions.summary: Students answer that Jephthah lacked circumspection and should have used forgiveness rather than literal fidelity, and Jiang endorses the point: Beatrice wants him to forgive himself for the rash promise instead of killing his daughter.
A student answers Jiang by comparing the choice to Dante's hell-structure: murdering one's daughter and betraying kin would put Jephthah far lower than simply breaking a promise to God.

claims.claim: Jiang keeps the packet centered on a paradox: Beatrice says to take vows seriously and not be like Jephthah, even though Jephthah appears to have taken his vow too seriously rather than too lightly.

A student proposes that God gave human beings enough understanding and free will to prevent rash promises in the first place, framing moral intelligence as a kind of preventative safeguard against Jephthah-like vows.
One student resolves the paradox by saying Jephthah followed through with zero circumspection and rationality, so taking vows seriously must include judgment rather than mere literal obedience.
Another student, using Hannah Arendt's promise-and-forgiveness frame, argues that Jephthah should have forgiven himself for breaking the promise instead of honoring it through murder.
Jiang explicitly endorses that reading of Beatrice: Jephthah made the promise rashly, so the right response was to forgive himself and not kill his daughter.

A student argues from Inferno that killing one's daughter and committing treachery against kin is worse than breaking a vow to God, so the lesser evil is to break the promise rather than descend deeper into hell through murder.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang states the contradiction in its hardest form: Beatrice says take vows seriously and do not be like the man who took his vow too seriously.
signature_moments.source_phrase: who took his vows too seriously
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the packet's central knot instead of flattening the discussion into generic advice about moderation or prudence.

signature_moments.moment: A student reaches for a medical image: God gives understanding as a vaccine or prevention shot against catastrophic vows.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The metaphor shows the class trying to preserve free will and divine order by turning judgment into prophylaxis rather than post-facto obedience.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang compresses the whole lesson into a blunt command: forgive yourself and do not kill your daughter for a rash promise.
signature_moments.source_phrase: forgive yourself and not kill your daughter man
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It keeps the packet ethically hot and makes the Arendt-to-Dante bridge usable for the later public read.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The rational, retrospective judgment a person must apply to a vow so literal fidelity does not become moral stupidity.
The Inferno frame the student uses to rank killing one's daughter as a deeper betrayal than merely breaking a promise to God.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-06-16 packet immediately stress-tests the prior Arendt praise of promise-making by elevating forgiveness and moral ranking above blind vow-keeping, then pulling Inferno's hell hierarchy into the discussion as an interpretive check.
